title: Goose v2 Necks
eyebrow: Design for approval · Models #18, the necks after your QA check · nothing changed in the model yet

short.lead: You said the version 2 necks still look like rigid, smooth tubes, and asked for necks that can move and show their vertebrae, like a real Canada goose's. A goose's neck has 17 to 18 vertebrae and bends in three regions, which is why it rests in an S. I ran a throwaway test that gives each neck an S-curve and vertebra ridges, without moving the heads. The pictures are untextured. Three questions follow.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it changes and why.
items: What a real Canada goose neck does

A goose's neck has 17 to 18 vertebrae (Frontiers in Veterinary Science, 2025, on domestic geese). The vertebrae are longest in the middle of the neck and shorter at both ends. The neck bends in three regions: the base leans forward, the middle bends back and up, and the top tips forward to the head. Together those bends make the resting S shape. On a thin bird, the vertebrae show along the back and sides of the neck, while the front, over the windpipe, stays smooth.
Show the vertebrae as ridges under the skin

Each neck swells slightly at every joint between vertebrae and narrows in the middle of each vertebra. The swelling is strongest along the back, with smaller bumps on each side where the side processes of the bone sit. The front stays smooth. The test uses 15 vertebrae on the main neck above the root and 12 on each side neck, which adds no triangles, so the skin stays within its 75,000 cap.

items: Rest the necks in an S-curve

In the current version 2 model each neck runs in a gentle straight line from the root to its head. In the test, each neck leans forward low, bends back in the middle and tips forward to the head, like an alert goose. The heads stay where they are, so the height stays 6.75 m.

items: The necks can only bend where the rig has bones. Today the main neck has 7 bones and each side neck has 6, so each bone would carry two or three vertebrae and the ridges would stretch as the neck bends. With one bone per vertebra (15 and 12), every joint can bend on its own and the neck can coil. This is built in #21 (the rig), but deciding it now sets how the ridges are spaced.
Your answer to "How many bones should each neck get in #21?"
